lessons.title: `Box<T>` and recursive types
lessons.book_section: 15.1 Using `Box<T>` to Point to Data on the Heap
lessons.objective_md: Put a value on the heap with `Box<T>`, and use boxes to give recursive types a known size.

screens.heading: A value on the heap
screens.text_md:
A **smart pointer** is a value that acts like a pointer but also owns what it points to and carries extra behaviour. `Box<T>` is the simplest: `Box::new(5)` puts the `5` on the heap, and `b`, on the stack, holds a pointer to it.

`b` prints like the value it holds. When `b` goes out of scope, both the box and the value it points to are freed, as with any owner.

coming_from.c: Like `std::unique_ptr<T>`: one owner, freed automatically. Moving the box moves ownership, and the old binding can't be used.
coming_from.go: Like a pointer from `new(T)`, but freed when its single owner goes out of scope instead of by the garbage collector.
coming_from.java: Like `new` for an object, except a `Box` has exactly one owner and is freed the moment that owner goes away.
coming_from.js: Objects are always heap references in JavaScript. `Box<T>` is how Rust opts in to a heap allocation, with one owner and no garbage collector.
coming_from.python: Every Python object already lives on the heap behind a reference. In Rust you choose: values live on the stack unless you box them.

screens.heading: Boxes are owners
screens.text_md:
`let b = a;` moves the box: the pointer is copied to `b` and `a` can no longer be used, while the `String` on the heap stays where it is. Moving a box is cheap however big its contents are.

`*c` reaches the value inside, for reading or, through a `mut` box, for changing. Methods work directly: `b.len()` calls the `String`'s method through the box.

question.prompt_md: `let b = Box::new(7);` Where are the `7` and `b`?

options.text_md: The `7` is on the heap; `b`, a pointer to it, is on the stack.
The `7` is on the stack; `b` is on the heap.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `Box::new` moves its argument into a heap allocation and returns the pointer that owns it.
Not quite. Putting the value on the heap is the whole point of a box.
Not quite. The box itself is an ordinary local variable.
Not quite. It's the other way round.

screens.heading: A type that contains itself
screens.text_md: This is the Book's **cons list**: each item holds a value and the rest of the list. Written directly, the type would contain itself and have no finite size (**E0072**). The fix the compiler suggests is the one to use: put the rest of the list behind a `Box`.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0072]: recursive type `List` has infinite size
 --> src/main.rs:1:1
  |
1 | enum List {
  | ^^^^^^^^^
2 |     Cons(i32, List),
  |               ---- recursive without indirection
  |
help: insert some indirection (e.g., a `Box`, `Rc`, or `&`) to break the cycle
  |
2 |     Cons(i32, Box<List>),
  |               ++++    +

annotations.note_md: line 2: a `Cons` holds a whole `List`, which may hold another `Cons`, and so on: the compiler can't work out how much space one `List` needs.
line 2: a `Box<List>` is a pointer, so its size is known whatever list it points to.

screens.heading: The cons list with `Box`
screens.text_md: Now a `Cons` is an `i32` plus a pointer, so every `List` has the same size. The list is a chain of heap allocations, each owning the next; `Nil` ends it. When `list` is dropped, each box drops the one after it.

question.prompt_md: `enum Tree { Leaf, Node(i32, Tree, Tree) }` compiles.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. A `Node` would contain two whole `Tree`s, so the type has no finite size (E0072).
Correct. `Node(i32, Box<Tree>, Box<Tree>)` fixes it: each child is a pointer.

screens.heading: Walking a recursive type
screens.text_md: Functions over recursive types follow their shape: one `match` arm for the case that holds more (`Cons`) and one for the end (`Nil`). `rest` is a `&Box<List>`; passing it where `&List` is expected works by deref coercion (L15.2).

screens.heading: When to use `Box`

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank so the tree type has a known size.
question.general_md: Each child becomes a pointer to a heap-allocated `Tree`, so a `Node` is an `i32` plus two pointers.

wrong_answers.why_md: that would compile too, but it's a growable list, not a single child.

summary: `Box<T>` puts a value on the heap; the box is its single owner and frees it when dropped.
`*b` reaches the value; methods work through the box directly. Moving a box moves ownership cheaply.
A type can't contain itself directly (E0072); `Box` gives a recursive type a known size.
Functions on recursive types match the "more" case and the "end" case.

lessons.title: `Deref` and deref coercion
lessons.book_section: 15.2 Treating Smart Pointers Like Regular References with `Deref`
lessons.objective_md: Make your own type work with `*` by implementing `Deref`, and recognise where Rust converts references for you.

screens.heading: Following a pointer
screens.text_md: `*y` **dereferences** a reference: it follows the pointer to the value. A `Box` works with `*` the same way. Without the `*`, `assert_eq!(5, y)` wouldn't compile, because a number and a reference to a number are different types.

screens.heading: Your own smart pointer
screens.text_md:
`MyBox` holds its value in a tuple field (not on the heap; that part isn't what matters here). Implementing the **`Deref`** trait tells Rust how to follow it: `deref` returns a reference to the inside, and `type Target` names what it points to.

Now `*y` works: Rust turns it into `*(y.deref())`. It still ends with a plain `*` on a reference, so the value isn't moved out of `y`.

coming_from.c: Like overloading `operator*` (and `operator->`) for a smart pointer class.
coming_from.go: Go dereferences pointers with `*` too, but you can't make your own types act like pointers.
coming_from.java: Java has no operator overloading. C# lets you overload some operators, but not dereferencing; Rust's `Deref` is the trait behind `*`.
coming_from.js: There's no dereferencing in JavaScript. Think of `Deref` as declaring "this wrapper stands for that value".
coming_from.python: Python has no pointers to dereference. The closest idea is a wrapper class that forwards attribute access with `__getattr__`.

question.prompt_md: What does `*y` mean when `y` is a `MyBox<i32>` that implements `Deref`?

options.text_md: Move the `i32` out of `y`, leaving it empty.
A compile error: `*` only works on references.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Rust calls `deref` to get a `&i32`, then dereferences that.
Not quite. `deref` returns a reference, so nothing is moved out.
Not quite. Dereferencing reaches the inside; it doesn't copy the wrapper.
Not quite. `*` works on anything that implements `Deref`.

screens.heading: Deref coercion
screens.text_md:
`hello` wants a `&str`, and `&m` is a `&MyBox<String>`. Rust converts it for you, calling `deref` as many times as needed: `&MyBox<String>` → `&String` → `&str`. This is **deref coercion**. Without it you'd write `hello(&(*m)[..])`.

The conversions are worked out at compile time, so they cost nothing when the program runs.

screens.heading: Changing through a pointer: `DerefMut`
screens.text_md: `Deref` gives shared access; **`DerefMut`** gives mutable access, so `*c += 1` can change the inside. It requires `Deref` with the same `Target`, and it works only through a mutable binding or a `&mut` reference.

question.prompt_md: Deref coercion can turn a `&Box<String>` into a `&str`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Rust applies `Deref` twice: `Box<String>` to `String`, then `String` to `str`.
Not quite. Coercion repeats `deref` as many times as needed to reach the expected type.

screens.heading: The three coercion rules
No mutable access from a shared one
screens.text_md: To change the number, the function needs `&mut`, and that has to come from a mutable binding: `let mut b = Box::new(5u32); add_one(&mut b);` works, by the second coercion rule.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/main.rs:8:13
  |
8 |     add_one(r);
  |     ------- ^ types differ in mutability
  |     |
  |     arguments to this function are incorrect
  |
  = note: expected mutable reference `&mut u32`
                     found reference `&Box<u32>`

annotations.note_md: line 8: coercion can follow `Box` to `u32`, but it can't turn a shared `&` into `&mut`.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank with the associated type that says what `MyBox<T>` points to.
question.general_md: `type Target = T;` tells Rust what `*` reaches and what deref coercion converts to. The program prints `3`.

wrong_answers.why_md: that's `Iterator`'s associated type.
that belongs to the arithmetic operator traits.

summary: `*` follows a reference, a `Box`, or any type that implements `Deref`.
`Deref::deref` returns a reference to the inside; `*x` means `*(x.deref())`, so nothing is moved out.
Deref coercion converts `&Wrapper` to `&Inner` at call sites, as many steps as needed: `&Box<String>` → `&str`.
`DerefMut` allows changes through `*`; shared references never coerce to mutable ones.

lessons.title: `Drop`
lessons.book_section: 15.3 Running Code on Cleanup with the `Drop` Trait
lessons.objective_md: Run code when a value is cleaned up, and know when that happens.

screens.heading: Code that runs at cleanup
screens.text_md:
The **`Drop`** trait has one method, `drop`, which Rust calls automatically when a value goes out of scope. That's how a `Box` frees its memory, and how a file closes itself.

At the end of `main`, the values are dropped in **reverse order of creation**: `_d` first, then `_c`.

coming_from.c: Exactly a C++ destructor (RAII): runs at scope end, in reverse order of construction.
coming_from.go: Like a `defer` that's attached to the value instead of written in each function.
coming_from.java: Like `close()` called automatically by try-with-resources, or `Dispose` in a `using` block, but for every value, with no special syntax.
coming_from.js: JavaScript has no destructors; cleanup is up to you. `Drop` makes cleanup automatic and predictable.
coming_from.python: Like `__del__`, except Rust runs it at a known moment (the end of the owner's scope), not whenever the garbage collector gets to it. Closer to a `with` block's `__exit__`.

panels.title: $ cargo run
panels.text:
CustomSmartPointers created
Dropping CustomSmartPointer with data `other stuff`!
Dropping CustomSmartPointer with data `my stuff`!

screens.heading: Dropping early
screens.text_md: To clean something up before the end of its scope (releasing a lock, say), pass it to **`std::mem::drop`**, which is in the prelude as `drop`. It takes ownership of the value and returns at once, so the value is dropped right there.

panels.title: $ cargo run
panels.text:
CustomSmartPointer created
Dropping CustomSmartPointer with data `some data`!
CustomSmartPointer dropped before the end of main

question.prompt_md: What does this program print?
question.general_md: Both values live until the end of `main`, after `end` is printed; then they're dropped in reverse order of creation.

wrong_answers.why_md: local variables are dropped last-created first.
nothing is dropped until the scope ends.

screens.heading: You can't call `drop` yourself
screens.text_md: The `drop` *method* is only for Rust to call. The `drop` *function* takes ownership, so after `drop(c)` there's no `c` left for Rust to clean up again.
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0040]: explicit use of destructor method
  --> src/main.rs:15:7
   |
15 |     c.drop();
   |       ^^^^ explicit destructor calls not allowed
   |
help: consider using `drop` function
   |
15 -     c.drop();
15 +     drop(c);
   |

annotations.note_md: line 15: Rust would still call `drop` again at the end of `main`, cleaning up the same value twice. Calling the method directly is forbidden (**E0040**).

screens.heading: Replacing a value drops the old one
screens.text_md: Assigning to a variable that already holds a value drops the old value first. A function returning a value moves it out, so it isn't dropped at the end of the function but by whoever ends up owning it.

panels.title: $ cargo run
panels.text:
assigning
drop old
assigned
drop new

question.prompt_md: Why is `c.drop()` an error, while `drop(c)` is fine?

options.text_md: `drop(c)` takes ownership, so Rust won't drop `c` again at the end of the scope; calling the method would leave `c` to be dropped twice.
Methods can't be called on structs that implement traits.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Ownership makes the double cleanup impossible: after `drop(c)`, `c` has moved away.
Not quite. Trait methods are called on structs all the time.
Not quite. `drop(c)` drops `c` at once, which runs its `Drop` code.
Not quite. There's no way to call the destructor method directly.

screens.heading: What `Drop` is for
Dropping in a loop
screens.text_md: A loop body is a scope too: each pass creates a new value and drops it at the end of that pass, before the next one starts.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank so the value is cleaned up before `"after"` is printed.
question.general_md: `drop(n)` moves `n` into a function that lets it go at once, so `cleaned` comes before `after`.

wrong_answers.why_md: calling the method directly is E0040.
Rust has no `free` function; ownership does the freeing.

summary: `Drop::drop` runs automatically when a value goes out of scope; locals are dropped in reverse order of creation.
`drop(value)` (`std::mem::drop`) drops a value early by taking ownership of it; calling `value.drop()` is forbidden (E0040).
Assigning a new value drops the old one; returned values are dropped by their new owner.
Each value is dropped exactly once.

lessons.title: `Rc<T>`: shared ownership
lessons.objective_md: Give one value several owners with `Rc<T>`, and follow its reference count.

screens.heading: Two owners don't fit in a `Box`
screens.text_md: The Book wants two lists, `b` and `c`, that both continue with `a`. With `Box`, `a` can belong to only one of them (**E0382**). Borrowing would need lifetimes tying `a` to both. The answer is shared ownership.

annotations.note_md: line 11: `c` wants to own `a` too, but a value has one owner.

coming_from.c: Like `std::shared_ptr` without atomic counting (single-threaded), and without a way to mutate the shared value directly.
coming_from.go: Like sharing a pointer, but ownership is counted and the value is freed the moment the count hits zero.
coming_from.java: Like sharing an object reference, freed deterministically when the last `Rc` is dropped rather than by the GC.
coming_from.js: Like any object that several variables refer to, but freed exactly when the last reference goes, not by a garbage collector.
coming_from.python: Python counts references to every object behind the scenes. `Rc` is that, opted into for one value, with the count visible through `Rc::strong_count`.

question.prompt_md: What does `Rc::clone(&a)` do?

options.text_md: Makes another owner of the same value and adds one to the count.
Copies the value into a new allocation.
Makes a weak reference that doesn't own the value.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Only the pointer is copied; the data is shared.
Not quite. That's what `clone` on the value itself would do; `Rc::clone` is cheap.
Not quite. `a` stays a valid owner.
Not quite. That's `Rc::downgrade` (L15.7).

screens.heading: Watching the count
screens.text_md: Each `Rc::clone` adds one; each owner dropped (here `c`, at the end of its block) subtracts one. Every owner reports the same count, because they share it. You never decrease the count yourself: dropping an `Rc` does it.

panels.title: $ cargo run
panels.text:
count after creating a = 1
count after creating b = 2
count after creating c = 3
count after c goes out of scope = 2

screens.heading: Same allocation, or equal values?
screens.text_md: `==` compares the values: `a` and `c` both hold 5. **`Rc::ptr_eq`** compares the allocations: only `a` and `b` share one. When identity matters (is this the same account? the same node?), use `ptr_eq`.

question.general_md: `a` and the two clones in the vector make 3 owners; dropping the vector drops both clones.

wrong_answers.why_md: the original `a` counts too.
dropping the vector drops the `Rc`s inside it.

screens.heading: `Rc` doesn't allow changes
screens.text_md: `Rc` only implements `Deref`, not `DerefMut`: shared ownership means shared, read-only access, matching the borrowing rules. To change shared data, put a `RefCell` inside, as L15.6 does.

error[E0596]: cannot borrow data in an `Rc` as mutable

6 |     b.push_str(" there");
  |     ^ cannot borrow as mutable
  |
  = help: trait `DerefMut` is required to modify through a dereference, but it is not implemented for `Rc<String>`

annotations.note_md: line 6: several owners share the `String`, so changing it through one would surprise the others.

screens.heading: When to use `Rc`

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank to print how many owners `data` has.
question.general_md: `Rc::strong_count` returns the number of owning `Rc`s, here 2.

summary: `Rc<T>` lets one value have several owners; it's freed when the last one is dropped.
`Rc::clone(&a)` adds an owner cheaply; `Rc::strong_count` shows how many there are.
`==` compares values; `Rc::ptr_eq` checks whether two `Rc`s share one allocation.
`Rc` gives shared, read-only access, and only within one thread.

lessons.title: `RefCell<T>` and interior mutability
lessons.objective_md: Change a value through a shared reference with `RefCell<T>`, which checks the borrowing rules while the program runs.

screens.heading: Changing through `&`
screens.text_md:
`add` gets only a shared reference, yet it changes the number. **`RefCell<T>`** allows that: `borrow_mut()` hands out mutable access to the value inside, and `borrow()` shared access. This is **interior mutability**: the type itself, not the reference you hold, controls changes.

The borrowing rules still apply (one `&mut` or any number of `&`), but `RefCell` checks them **while the program runs** instead of at compile time.

coming_from.c: Like a `mutable` member changed from a `const` method, but checked: overlapping access panics instead of being undefined.
coming_from.go: Like changing a struct through a shared pointer, with a built-in single-threaded check against conflicting access.
coming_from.java: Like a field you can change through a final/readonly reference, plus a runtime check that throws on conflicting access.
coming_from.js: Like a `const` binding to an object whose contents can still change, with a runtime guard against overlapping writes.
coming_from.python: Python objects can always be changed through any reference. `RefCell` brings that flexibility to Rust, but keeps a running check that nobody reads while someone writes.

screens.heading: Borrow guards
screens.text_md:
`borrow()` returns a `Ref<T>` and `borrow_mut()` a `RefMut<T>`: **guards** that act like `&T` and `&mut T`. While a guard exists, the cell counts it; when the guard is dropped, the borrow ends. Several `Ref`s at once are fine; a `RefMut` must be alone.

Here the two readers end at the block's end, so the `push` can borrow mutably.

question.prompt_md: When does `RefCell<T>` check the borrowing rules?

options.text_md: While the program runs, each time `borrow` or `borrow_mut` is called.
At compile time, like ordinary references.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The cell counts its active guards and refuses a conflicting borrow.
Not quite. Moving the check to run time is exactly what `RefCell` does.
Not quite. The rules still hold; breaking them panics.
Not quite. The check runs in every build.

screens.heading: Breaking the rules panics
screens.text_md:
This compiles: the compiler doesn't track `RefCell` borrows. But two mutable borrows at once break the rules, so the second `borrow_mut` **panics** when the program runs.

That's the price of `RefCell`: a mistake the compiler would have caught becomes a crash at run time, possibly only on some inputs. Keep guards short-lived to avoid it.

panels.title: $ cargo run
panels.text:
thread 'main' panicked at src/main.rs:6:23:
RefCell already borrowed

screens.heading: Asking instead of panicking
screens.text_md: `try_borrow_mut()` (and `try_borrow()`) return a `Result` instead of panicking: `Err` when the borrow would conflict. Use them when a conflict is a situation you expect and can handle, not a bug.

question.prompt_md: What does this program print?
question.general_md: While `r` reads, a mutable borrow is refused but another shared borrow is fine. After `drop(r)`, nothing blocks the mutable borrow.

wrong_answers.why_md: a reader blocks writers.
any number of readers may share the cell.

screens.heading: The Book's mock object
screens.text_md: The `Messenger` trait's `send` takes `&self`, which is right for real messengers. A test double that wants to **record** messages needs to change itself, though. Wrapping its list in a `RefCell` lets `send` push through `&self` without changing the trait.

screens.heading: `Box`, `Rc` or `RefCell`?
screens.text_md:
| | Owners | Borrow rules checked | Change the value through |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Box<T>` | one | at compile time | a mutable box |
| `Rc<T>` | several | at compile time | (no changes) |
| `RefCell<T>` | one | at run time | a shared reference to the cell |

`RefCell` is single-threaded, like `Rc`. Reach for it only when the compiler's checks are too strict for a design you know is correct, such as a method that must take `&self`. The next lesson combines `Rc` and `RefCell` for shared data that can change.

question.prompt_md: Fill in the blank so `log` can record through `&self`.
question.general_md: `borrow_mut()` gives a guard that acts like `&mut Vec<String>`, so `push` works. The program prints `1`.

wrong_answers.why_md: a shared borrow can't push.
that needs `&mut self`, which `log` doesn't have.

summary: `RefCell<T>` allows changing its value through a shared reference: interior mutability.
`borrow()` and `borrow_mut()` return guards; the borrow lasts until the guard is dropped.
The borrowing rules are checked at run time: a conflicting `borrow_mut` panics; `try_borrow_mut` returns an `Err` instead.
Use it when an API fixes `&self` but the type must change something inside, as mock objects do.

lessons.title: `Rc<RefCell<T>>`: shared, changeable data
lessons.book_section: 15.5 `RefCell<T>` and the Interior Mutability Pattern (multiple owners of mutable data)
lessons.objective_md: Give a value several owners who can all change it, and keep the borrows short.

screens.heading: Several owners, one changeable value
screens.text_md: `Rc` gives several owners; `RefCell` lets one of them change the value. Together, **`Rc<RefCell<T>>`**, any owner can change the one shared value, and every owner sees the change. `team_a.borrow_mut()` works because `Rc` derefs to the `RefCell`.

coming_from.c: Like a `std::shared_ptr` to an object with a checked lock-free borrow flag; single-threaded only.
coming_from.go: Like several pointers to one struct, but with ownership counted and conflicting access detected.
coming_from.java: Like sharing one mutable object between several classes, with the access rules checked at run time.
coming_from.js: Like several variables referring to one object and changing it, with a runtime guard against a write during a read.
coming_from.python: This is how every Python object behaves: shared and changeable. In Rust you ask for it explicitly, and still get a check against overlapping writes.

screens.heading: The Book's shared list
screens.text_md: Lists `b` and `c` share the tail `a`, and `a`'s value is an `Rc<RefCell<i32>>` that `value` also owns. Adding 10 through `value` changes what all three lists show.

panels.title: $ cargo run
panels.text:
a after = Cons(RefCell { value: 15 }, Nil)
b after = Cons(RefCell { value: 3 }, Cons(RefCell { value: 15 }, Nil))
c after = Cons(RefCell { value: 4 }, Cons(RefCell { value: 15 }, Nil))

question.prompt_md: Which type lets several owners share one `Vec<String>` that any of them can push to?

explanations.text_md: Correct. `Rc` for several owners, `RefCell` for changes through them.
Not quite. `Rc` alone allows no changes.
Not quite. A `RefCell` alone has one owner.
Not quite. A `Box` has one owner.

screens.heading: A copy is not a share
screens.text_md: `Rc::clone` makes another owner of the same `String`; cloning the `String` itself (`shared.borrow().clone()`) makes a separate text. Changes through `alias` show up in `shared`, never in `copy`.

screens.heading: Keep guards short
screens.text_md: `*count.borrow()` copies the number out, and the guard is dropped at the end of that statement, so the `borrow_mut` on the next line doesn't conflict. Had the first line kept the guard (`let seen = count.borrow();`) while the second borrowed mutably, the program would panic, even though `count` and `other` are different variables: they share one cell.

question.prompt_md: `a` and `b` are clones of the same `Rc<RefCell<u32>>`. Holding `let r = a.borrow();` while calling `b.borrow_mut()` panics.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Both handles reach one `RefCell`, which sees a mutable borrow during a shared one.
Not quite. The check belongs to the cell, not to the variable used to reach it.

screens.heading: Same account?
screens.text_md: Two parameters may be the same shared value. Borrowing it mutably twice would panic, so check identity with `Rc::ptr_eq` first. Moving points from an account to itself changes nothing anyway.

screens.heading: When to reach for it
screens.text_md:
`Rc<RefCell<T>>` is the Book's answer for single-threaded data with several owners that all need to change it: a shared counter, a graph whose nodes are updated, a model several views edit.

It comes with two costs: borrow conflicts appear only when the program runs, and every access goes through a check. Prefer plain ownership and `&mut` where they fit, and keep `RefCell` guards inside short functions. Across threads, the same pattern is `Arc<Mutex<T>>` (Chapter 16).

lessons.title: Reference cycles and `Weak<T>`
lessons.objective_md: Recognise how `Rc` cycles leak memory, and break them with `Weak<T>`.

screens.heading: A cycle that never ends
screens.text_md:
`b` owns `a`, and then `a` is made to own `b`: a **reference cycle**. Each has two owners. At the end of `main`, dropping the variables `a` and `b` brings each count down to 1, never to 0, so neither node is freed: the memory **leaks**.

Rust's guarantees don't rule this out: a leak is safe, just wasteful. Avoiding cycles is up to the design.

coming_from.c: Exactly the `std::shared_ptr` cycle problem, solved the same way: `std::weak_ptr` there, `Weak` here.
coming_from.go: Go's collector frees unreachable cycles. Rust's `Rc` can't; one direction must be `Weak`.
coming_from.java: The garbage collector handles cycles. With reference counting, cycles must be avoided by design, using weak references.
coming_from.js: The garbage collector frees cycles for you. With `Rc` there's no collector, so a cycle stays alive until the program ends.
coming_from.python: CPython's reference counting has the same problem, which is why it adds a cycle-detecting garbage collector. Rust has no such collector: you break cycles yourself, with `Weak`.

screens.heading: `Weak<T>`: a pointer that doesn't own
screens.text_md: `Rc::downgrade(&strong)` makes a **`Weak<T>`**: a pointer that knows where the value is but doesn't count as an owner. To use it, call `upgrade()`, which returns `Some(Rc<T>)` while the value is alive and `None` after it's been freed. Weak handles have their own count, `Rc::weak_count`, which doesn't keep the value alive.

screens.heading: Trees: strong down, weak up
screens.text_md: The Book's tree: a parent **owns** its children (strong `Rc`s in `children`), and a child **observes** its parent (a `Weak` in `parent`). The child can reach its parent, but doesn't keep it alive, so there's no cycle: dropping `branch` frees it, even though `leaf` points back at it.

When the block ends, `branch`'s strong count reaches zero, so it's freed, dropping its children vector: the leaf is back to one owner, and its parent link no longer upgrades.

problems.description_md:

1. Make a ticket `"outer"`.
2. In an inner block, make `"first"` and then `"second"`, then drop `"first"` early with `std::mem::drop(first)`.
3. Let the inner block end, then the function's body.

```text
Expected:   vec!["first".to_string(), "second".to_string(), "outer".to_string()]
```

2. `inorder(tree)` returns the values left subtree first, then the node, then the right subtree. For a tree built by `balanced`, that's the original slice.
3. `height(tree)` is the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down: 0 for `Empty`.

```text
Expected:   vec![3, 1, 2]
```

problems.title: Evaluate an owned expression tree
problems.description_md:
An arithmetic expression is a tree: a number, or an operation whose two operands are expressions themselves, in `Box`es.

1. `evaluate(expr)` computes the value with `i64` arithmetic. It evaluates the left operand, then the right, then applies the operation with overflow checking. Any overflow anywhere makes the result `Err("overflow")`, even if a later step would have brought the value back in range. `Sub` is subtraction; `Neg` negates its operand (`-i64::MIN` overflows).
2. `expression(a, b, c)` builds the tree for `(a + b) * c`.
3. `render(expr)` writes it fully bracketed: numbers as they are, `Add` as `(l + r)`, `Sub` as `(l - r)`, `Mul` as `(l * r)`, `Neg` as `-x`. Negative numbers are written with their sign, like `-3`.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::evaluate(&crate::expression(2, 3, 4))
Expected:   Ok(20)

Expression: crate::render(&crate::expression(2, 3, 4))
Expected:   "((2 + 3) * 4)".to_string()
```

problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::forest(&["ana", "bo", "cy"], &[None, Some(0), Some(1)])
Expected:   (vec!["ana".to_string()], vec!["ana".to_string(), "ana/bo".to_string(), "ana/bo/cy".to_string()], true)
```

hints: Make all the people first, in a `Vec<Rc<Person>>`; then link each `i` whose parent index is smaller.

problems.title: Transfer across shared accounts
problems.description_md:
Accounts are `Rc<RefCell<u32>>` balances that several parts of a program share. Write `transfer(from, to, amount)`, which moves `amount` from one account to the other **all or nothing**:

1. If `from` and `to` are the same account (`Rc::ptr_eq`), return `Ok(())` and change nothing: moving money to itself is a no-op, whatever the amount.
2. Borrow `from` mutably, then `to`, each with `try_borrow_mut`; if either is already borrowed elsewhere, return `Err("busy")`.
3. If `from` has less than `amount`, return `Err("funds")`; if `to` would go past `u32::MAX`, return `Err("overflow")`.
4. Otherwise move the money and return `Ok(())`.

Every error leaves both balances unchanged. Check in this order: busy, funds, overflow.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let a = std::rc::Rc::new(std::cell::RefCell::new(10)); let b = std::rc::Rc::new(std::cell::RefCell::new(0)); let r = crate::transfer(&a, &b, 4); (r, *a.borrow(), *b.borrow()) }
Expected:   (Ok(()), 6, 4)
```
problems.constraints_md: - Any `u32` balances and amounts. No `unwrap()` or panics: two `borrow_mut`s of the same cell would panic.
hints: Check `Rc::ptr_eq(from, to)` first: borrowing the same cell twice would fail.
`let mut a = from.try_borrow_mut().map_err(|_| "busy")?;` and the same for `to`.
`if *a < amount { return Err("funds"); }`, `let new_b = b.checked_add(amount).ok_or("overflow")?;`, then write both.
problems.solution_approach_md: The identity check comes first because the same `RefCell` can't be mutably borrowed twice. `try_borrow_mut` with `map_err` turns a conflict into `"busy"`. Both guards are held while checking and writing, so nothing else can change the balances in between; every check happens before any write, which is what makes failures leave both untouched.
problems.idiomatic_md: Acquire everything, check everything, then change everything: the same shape keeps transfers consistent with locks in Chapter 16.

The case's result is `(result, balance of from, balance of to)` after the call. Use the common generator, seed `0x0F000019`, exactly 300 cases.

problems.title: Family tree with weak parents
problems.comes_after: All chapter lessons and one Medium Accepted
problems.description_md:
Build a family tree in the library package `family`. People are `Rc<Person>`: a person owns their children strongly and observes their parent weakly, so the tree never forms an ownership cycle. The `parent` and `children` fields are private; everything goes through the functions below.

**Part 1 · People and links**

- `person(name)` makes a person with no parent and no children.
- `attach(parent, child)` makes `child` a child of `parent`: it's added to the parent's children (strongly) and its parent link is set (weakly). It returns `Ok(())`. (Part 2 adds the rules.)
- `parent_name(person)` is the parent's name, or `None` when there's no live parent.
- `children_names(person)` lists the children's names, sorted; equal names are kept.

**Part 2 · Rules for attaching**

`attach` now checks, in this order, and changes nothing when it fails:

1. `Err("cycle")` if `child` is `parent` itself or one of `parent`'s ancestors.
2. `Ok(())` without changes if `child`'s live parent is already `parent`.
3. `Err("parented")` if `child` has another live parent.

**Part 3 · Detaching and ancestry**

- `detach(parent, child)` removes the link if `child`'s parent is `parent` (compare allocations, not names): it removes that exact child from the children, resets the child's parent link and returns `true`. Otherwise it returns `false` and changes nothing.
- `ancestors(person)` lists the names of the parent, grandparent, and so on, nearest first.

**Part 4 · Lifetimes**

Nothing new to write: the rows of this part check that the tree frees memory correctly. When the last owner of a parent is dropped, a child held elsewhere survives, and its parent link expires. No cycles keep people alive.

hints: `fn parent_of(p: &Rc<Person>) -> Option<Rc<Person>> { p.parent.borrow().upgrade() }` is a handy helper; the borrow ends inside it.

problems.solution_approach_md: All links go through two small operations: pushing a strong child handle and setting a weak parent handle. A helper upgrades the parent, so every borrow ends at once. The cycle check walks up from the new parent; if it meets the child, linking would make the child its own ancestor. `detach` compares allocations with `ptr_eq` so equal names never get confused, and `ancestors` repeats the upward walk, collecting names.
problems.idiomatic_md: Private fields plus functions that keep both directions in step are what make the invariant hold: a child appears in a parent's list exactly when its weak link points back to that parent.

problems.title: Household accounts
problems.description_md:
Families share a library account: one **household** pays its members' late fees. The starter is the LM14 workspace with a new module, `core/src/households.rs` (`pub mod households;` is already in `core/src/lib.rs`). A household is shared, so it's a `HouseholdRef`, an `Rc<RefCell<Household>>`. It lists its members with **weak** handles to `Rc<RefCell<Member>>`s: the household never keeps a member alive. The rest of the library is unchanged.

**Part 1 · Households and balances**

- `new_household(name)` makes a household with that name and a balance of 0 cents.
- `balance(h)` reads the balance; `charge(h, cents)` adds to it, stopping at `u32::MAX`.

**Part 2 · Members**

- `join(h, member)` adds a weak handle to `member`; if that same member (the same allocation) is already listed and alive, it returns `false` and adds nothing, otherwise `true`.
- `member_names(h)` lists the names of the members that are still alive, sorted.
- `prune(h)` removes the handles of members that are gone and returns how many it removed.

**Part 3 · Late fees**

`charge_late(h, due_day, return_day)` works out the fee with the library's own rules, `fees::late_fee_cents(fees::days_late(due_day, return_day))`, charges it to the household and returns it. The command-line program still works as in LM14.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let h = crate::households::new_household("Smith"); crate::households::charge(&h, 250); crate::households::balance(&h) }
Expected:   250
```
problems.constraints_md: - Up to 10,000 members per household. No `unwrap()`. The household holds only `Weak` member handles.
hints: `h.borrow().balance_cents` reads; `let mut hh = h.borrow_mut(); hh.balance_cents = hh.balance_cents.saturating_add(cents);` writes.
`join`: `if hh.members.iter().any(|w| w.upgrade().is_some_and(|m| Rc::ptr_eq(&m, member))) { return false; }`, then `hh.members.push(Rc::downgrade(member));`.
`member_names`: upgrade each handle with `filter_map`, read `m.borrow().name.clone()`, then sort; `prune` uses `retain` and compares lengths.
problems.solution_approach_md: `HouseholdRef` lets several parts of the program share one household; `RefCell` lets them change its balance and member list. Members are listed as `Weak`s, so the library's own `Rc` handles stay the only owners: when a member goes, the handle stops upgrading, `member_names` skips it, and `prune` clears it. `charge_late` reuses the fee rules from `fees` instead of copying them.
problems.idiomatic_md: `type HouseholdRef = Rc<RefCell<Household>>;` names a pattern you'd otherwise repeat everywhere, and makes signatures read like the domain.
